summary: Presents a checklist for evaluating MIME-capable user agents. It replaces RFC 1820 with an updated version. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1844 is a checklist for evaluating email programs that support MIME, the extension that lets a message carry pictures, sound and other file types. It asks about the product, its installation, the everyday mail functions and its MIME support. A test responder described in the memo returns a message of any content type the tester asks for, so the answers can be checked against a real message.

subtitle: A questionnaire for judging how well an email program handles MIME, plus a responder that mails you test messages.

tldr.problem: People choosing an email program had no way to compare how well different products handled MIME, the extension that carries pictures, sound and other file types inside a message.
tldr.mechanism: The memo gives a questionnaire of about a hundred items in four groups, covering the product, its installation, the user's everyday mail functions and its MIME support, and it describes a test responder that returns a message of any requested content type.
tldr.outcome: Filled-in checklists could be submitted by mail and published for others to browse, so buyers had a shared set of answers to compare products by.

today: RFC 1844 is an Informational memo published in August 1995, and it has not been obsoleted or updated. It revises the earlier checklist in RFC 1820 and points to the MIME standards RFC 1521 and RFC 1522 for the format being tested.

sections.title: What the Checklist Is For
sections.content:
The memo presents a checklist that facilitates the evaluation of MIME capable email user agents. It is by no means a conformance or interoperability checklist, both of which are strictly defined and measurable quantities. It is an interworking checklist, a practical perspective, aimed at users and system managers.

The questionnaire is organised in four groups: general information about the product, system installation, configuration and management, general user agent properties, and MIME support. Several items offer multiple choices, and the memo notes that for those it is possible that more than one option is applicable.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo is a questionnaire for judging how well an email program handles MIME, the extension that lets a message carry pictures, sound and other file types. It is aimed at people choosing or running mail software, not at testing a product against the MIME standard.

sections.title: Submitting a Filled-In Checklist
sections.content:
A filled-in checklist for a specific product can be submitted by mail to mime-check@nic.surfnet.nl, with the subject field reflecting the name and version of the product. The address is an automated mail handler, so only filled-in checklists, in content type text/plain or text/html, should be sent to it. The information is then made available, at no cost, for other people to browse through.

Although SURFnet will attempt to verify the correctness of each submission, all submitted information is made available as is, with no guarantees. Users who want to procure a user agent are advised to use the data as an orientation and to perform their own procurement tests, possibly using the checklist as a guideline. Vendors and implementors are encouraged to use the results from the checklist to improve their products.
sections.plainLanguage: You send your completed questionnaire to a mailbox that files the results for others to read. The results are published as they arrive, so anyone shopping for mail software should still run their own tests rather than rely on them.

sections.title: Requesting Test Messages
sections.content:
Several items in the checklist need a test message. Test messages are requested by sending mail to mime-test@relay.surfnet.nl with a subject field containing one of a list of content types. The list covers text/plain, text/enriched, image/gif, image/jpeg, audio/basic, video/mpeg, application/octet-stream and application/postscript, the message/rfc822, message/partial and message/external types, the multipart/mixed, multipart/parallel, multipart/digest, multipart/alternative and multipart/appledouble types, and types such as application/wordperfect5.1, application/msword and application/rtf.

Three further subjects are special. X-local tests how the user agent deals with undefined content types, nested returns a message that contains nested multipart contents, and iso-8859-1 returns a message with text/plain; charset=iso-8859-1. A message containing the requested content type is returned to the address contained in the From field.
sections.plainLanguage: Many of the questions need a real message to look at. You ask for one by mailing the test responder and putting the content type you want in the subject line. It sends the message back to the address you wrote in.

sections.title: What the Checklist Asks For
sections.content:
The first group asks for general information: the name and version of the product, the name and addressing information of the manufacturer, the platforms supported and the APIs used, the platform on which the checklist was filled in, whether the software is available in source, binary or both, and pricing information, with the software in the public domain, as shareware, as public domain for non-profit use only, or commercially.

The second group covers installation, configuration and management: how complex installation and configuration are, whether configuration can be system wide or per user, logging and accounting facilities, whether the user agent generates correct RFC 822 headers for outgoing messages, whether an unprivileged user can change the From or Sender field, size restrictions on messages, folders and messages per folder, how secure the user mailbox is against other unprivileged users, and a subjective impression of performance. The third group asks about general properties: the kind of interface, whether MIME is supported natively or needs a gateway, the protocols used for delivery and submission, the basic functions such as listing, reading, deleting, composing, replying, forwarding and distributing messages, the header fields supported and whether the user can supply them, filing into folders, filtering and sorting of incoming mail, address lists and directory services, other non-multimedia facilities, and secure mail protocols.

The fourth group is MIME support. It asks whether a MIME content can be viewed, saved, saved one part at a time and printed; which basic content types can be received, displayed in line and printed, and whether an external viewer is needed, preconfigured or included in the distribution; how the multipart types are handled and what happens with unknown or unconfigured content types; whether additional content types can be configured and whether the basic types can be composed; which content encodings are supported, being 7bit, quoted printable, base64, binary and 8bit, and which encoding is used for each content type; whether the correct Mime-Version: 1.0 header is generated; what a multipart boundary string looks like; whether non-ASCII characters may be used in headers; and which character sets are supported for plain text.
sections.plainLanguage: The questionnaire walks through who makes the product and what it costs, how it is installed and configured, what a user can do with mail, and then MIME itself: which types it can show and print, which it can create, and how it encodes them.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: Testing a MIME user agent against the checklist involves the security risks that are described in the MIME specification, RFC 1521. Most notably, the automatic execution of general-purpose PostScript interpreters entails serious security risks. The reader is encouraged to read RFC 1521 for more detail on these security risks.
sections.plainLanguage: Opening a message can run code on the computer, and the memo singles out PostScript as the serious case. It sends the reader to the MIME specification for the details.

items.title: General information
items.text: Product name and version, manufacturer, platforms, source or binary, pricing.

items.title: Installation and management
items.text: How hard setup is, logging, outgoing RFC 822 headers, mailbox security, performance.

items.title: General user agent properties
items.text: Interface, delivery and submission protocols, filing, filtering, sorting, address lists, secure mail.

items.title: MIME support
items.text: Receiving, viewing, printing and composing content types, content encodings, headers, boundaries.
